decision.summary: 36 of 39 findings are evidence-backed; 3 were insufficient and recorded for follow-up.

findings.statement: Broadcom has publicly disclosed that major cloud and AI players are using its AI solutions: Google and Meta have multi‑year custom silicon contracts; OpenAI and Anthropic have strategic collaborations and financing agreements for AI accelerators; European cloud providers T‑Systems and OVHcloud partner with Broadcom’s VMware software stack for sovereign AI cloud services.

Broadcom’s AI‑computing offerings are sold under a bundled‑subscription licensing model for private AI services, with indications that usage‑based billing options will be added. The company promotes a cost model that can be 3–5 times cheaper than comparable public‑cloud AI services, emphasizing predictable subscription pricing versus token‑based billing used by public providers.

Broadcom: VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.0 now includes VMware Private AI Services as a standard component, offering native AI capabilities such as GPU Monitoring, Model Store, Model Runtime, Agent Builder, Vector Database, and Data Indexing/Retrieval for secure private‑cloud AI workloads.

Broadcom: CloudHealth, Broadcom’s multi‑cloud FinOps platform, introduced an AI and Tokenomics Dashboard in 2026 that provides unified reporting, token‑consumption tracking and cost analytics for AI workloads across multiple LLM providers.

Broadcom: In October 2026 Broadcom announced a $63 billion financing structure with Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley to fund AI compute capacity, signalling forthcoming AI infrastructure offerings for cloud providers.
Broadcom: At FinOps X 2026 Broadcom launched the AI and Tokenomics Dashboard within CloudHealth, adding AI‑specific cost visibility and token‑usage analytics for enterprise AI workloads.

Broadcom’s licensing model separates primary licenses (e.g., VMware Cloud Foundation) from add‑on licenses such as VMware Private AI Foundation, with capacity allocated per core or per TiB and delivered via subscription.
AMD: The upcoming Instinct MI325X accelerator, announced for Q4 2024, will feature up to 288 GB of HBM3E memory to support large AI models and memory‑intensive workloads.
AMD provides the open‑source ROCm software stack, developer tools, SDKs and an AI Developer Program that enable developers to build, train and deploy AI models on AMD CPUs, GPUs and accelerators.
AMD offers Alveo accelerator cards and Pensando DPUs as part of its data‑center AI and networking acceleration portfolio, available through OEM and system‑integrator partners.
AMD: Microsoft Azure provides AMD‑powered virtual machines that use EPYC processors and Instinct GPUs for AI workloads, serving customers in both the United States and Europe.
AMD: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) runs AMD Instinct GPUs and EPYC CPUs for AI and HPC, with expanded availability of MI350‑based instances.
AMD: European cloud integrator Nscale operates a GPU cluster in Norway powered by AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators, delivering AI training, fine‑tuning and inference services.

AMD announced an expanded AI accelerator roadmap: MI325X (Q4 2024), MI350 series (2025) based on CDNA 4 architecture, and MI400 series (2026) based on the next‑generation CDNA architecture, each promising generational performance and memory improvements.

AMD unveiled the Helios rack‑scale AI infrastructure platform, which integrates CPUs, GPUs, DPUs and networking to deliver end‑to‑end AI compute at hyperscale, with initial deployments planned for 2025‑2026.
AMD: In July 2024 AMD announced the acquisition of Silo AI, Europe’s largest private AI lab, to expand end‑to‑end AI solutions and open‑source LLM development on AMD hardware.
AMD licenses its AI software through FlexNet, offering both node‑locked licenses (unlimited concurrent runs on a single machine) and floating/network‑floating licenses for multi‑user environments.

AMD offers the Instinct MI350 series GPUs, including the MI350P PCIe card, featuring up to 288 GB of HBM3E memory and 8 TB/s bandwidth, built on the 4th‑Gen CDNA architecture for generative AI training, inference and high‑performance computing.

AMD’s Instinct MI400 series GPUs (e.g., MI455X and MI430X) are positioned for frontier AI, sovereign AI and HPC, delivered via the Helios rack‑scale solution and supported by open ROCm software, virtualization and partitioning capabilities.

AMD EPYC 9004 processors are available in Google Cloud’s C3D VM series, delivering a 37 % performance uplift for AI workloads compared with the prior generation, enabling cloud‑based AI training and inference.

AMD: The Vitis Unified Software Platform (2026.1 release) provides a development environment for AI Engine, FPGA and CPU designs, with free AI Engine tools and optional Vivado Enterprise (perpetual) or Vivado Pro (subscription) licenses for hardware implementation.

findings.statement: AMD: Google Cloud offers C3D virtual machines built on AMD EPYC 9004 CPUs, providing cloud customers in Europe and the United States with AI‑optimized compute resources.

AMD: Anthropic, an AI development firm, has a strategic partnership to deploy up to 2 GW of AMD Instinct MI450 series GPUs in AMD Helios rack‑scale solutions, with the first gigawatt slated for the first half of 2027.
AMD: Vultr, a cloud‑infrastructure‑as‑a‑service provider, offers AI infrastructure powered by AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs, targeting AI developers and enterprises.
AMD released Vitis 2026.1, adding tiered licensing for the Vivado Design Suite and free AI Engine tools, signaling an enhanced software stack to support AI workloads on AMD hardware.

findings.statement: AMD’s Vitis platform licenses AI Engine tools at no cost, while hardware design flows require a Vivado Enterprise perpetual license or a Vivado Pro subscription; the 2026.1 release introduces tiered licensing so customers pay only for the device families they need.

findings.statement: Intel Corp: Intel provides a portfolio of AI computing hardware that includes 4th‑Gen Intel® Xeon® Scalable processors with Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), Xeon 6 and Xeon 6+ processors for data‑center and edge workloads, Intel® Gaudi 2 and Gaudi 3 AI accelerators, Intel® Arc GPUs, and Intel® Core Ultra processors for AI PCs. Complementary software platforms include Intel AI Solutions, the Intel® Tiber Developer Cloud, oneAPI development tools, and Intel® Deep Learning Boost optimizations for AI inference and training, all marketed to cloud service providers and AI developers in the United States and Europe.

Intel Corp: Major cloud service providers that have deployed Intel AI hardware in the United States and Europe include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, IBM Cloud (which offers Gaudi 3 instances in Frankfurt, Germany) and Oracle Cloud. AI development and consulting firms such as C3 IoT and Accenture are also highlighted as partners using Intel AI solutions for data‑center, cloud and edge AI workloads.

Intel Corp: Intel’s pricing model for its AI accelerators includes Gaudi 2 and Gaudi 3 accelerator kits sold at up to one‑third lower list price than competing platforms, and IBM Cloud offers Gaudi 3 instances at roughly 30 % lower hourly rates than comparable NVIDIA GPU instances. Intel also promotes a token‑per‑dollar metric to express cost efficiency for AI inference workloads on these cloud instances.

Intel Corp: Intel offers a portfolio of AI‑computing hardware that includes the Intel® Data Center GPU Flex Series (Flex 140 with 16 Xe cores and 12 GB memory; Flex 170 with 32 Xe cores and 16 GB memory), 4th‑ and 5th‑generation Intel® Xeon® Scalable processors, the Intel® Xeon® Max Series GPUs (1100 and 1550), and Habana® Gaudi 2 AI accelerators. These products are positioned for data‑center and edge deployments used by cloud service providers and AI developers in Europe and the United States.

Intel Corp: Intel’s AI software stack for cloud and AI developers is built around the open, standards‑based oneAPI ecosystem, including the oneAPI Base Toolkit, the Intel® Distribution of OpenVINO™ Toolkit, and the Intel® Device Plugins Operator that integrates Flex GPUs with Red Hat OpenShift Data Science (RHODS). The same stack underpins Intel® Developer Cloud and Tiber Developer Cloud, providing unified programming across CPUs, GPUs, and accelerators.

Intel Corp: AI startups such as Prediction Guard and Seekr are using Intel Tiber Developer Cloud to run production services on Intel CPUs, GPUs and Gaudi 2 accelerators, while leading AI‑development communities including Hugging Face, Google and the PyTorch Foundation collaborate with Intel to upstream performance optimizations into popular frameworks.

Intel Corp: In August 2022 Intel announced the Intel® Data Center GPU Flex Series, a new line of Xe‑HPG GPUs (Flex 140 and Flex 170) designed for AI inference, media transcoding, cloud gaming and VDI workloads, delivering up to 55 % better visual inference performance than the NVIDIA A10 and up to 5× media transcode throughput.

Intel Corp: Intel launched the Tiber Developer Cloud, a cloud‑native AI platform that provides bare‑metal access to Gaudi 2 accelerators, Xeon Scalable CPUs and Max Series GPUs, as well as VM and Kubernetes services, enabling developers to benchmark and deploy large‑language‑model workloads ahead of general availability.

Intel Corp: Intel’s recommended pricing for the Data Center GPU Flex Series is presented as a customer‑price that can reduce total cost of ownership by up to 50 % for VDI deployments compared with competing solutions, with actual system‑level costs varying by server configuration.

Intel Corp: The Intel Developer Cloud is offered in a free tier that provides limited cloud credits for selected instance types, and a premium enterprise tier billed on a pay‑as‑you‑go basis, allowing AI and HPC developers to scale usage and only pay for the compute resources consumed.
Intel Gaudi AI accelerators are identified as an AI‑computing alternative to NVIDIA’s offerings.
NVIDIA currently sells AI computing and data‑center platforms to cloud service providers and AI developers in the United States and Europe.
Broadcom’s AI‑accelerator offerings should be verified against its public reporting, as availability may be limited to specific customers or services.
